source.author: stat
source.text: Saevus at interea ferro post terga revinctas Antigonen viduamque Creon Arrastida leto admovet; ambae hilares et mortis amore superbae ensibus intentant iugulos regemque cruentum destituunt: eum dicta ferens Theseia Phegeus astitit, ille quidem ramis insontis olivae pacificus, sed bella ciet bellumque minatur, grande fremens,nimiumque memor mandantis et ipsum iam prope, iam medios operire cohortibus agros ingeminans, stetit ambiguo Thebanus in aestu curarum, nutantque minae et prior ira tepescit.
source.text_original: Saevus at interea ferro post terga revinctas / Antigonen viduamque Creon Arrastida leto / admovet; ambae hilares et mortis amore superbae / ensibus intentant iugulos regemque cruentum / destituunt: eum dicta ferens Theseia Phegeus / astitit, ille quidem ramis insontis olivae / pacificus, sed bella ciet bellumque minatur, / grande fremens,nimiumque memor mandantis et ipsum / iam prope, iam medios operire cohortibus agros / ingeminans, stetit ambiguo Thebanus in aestu / curarum, nutantque minae et prior ira tepescit.
source.text_english: Meanwhile the savage Creon, with iron fetters on their backs, drives Antigone and the widowed Arrastis to death; both, exultant and proud in their love of death, brandish their throats at the swords and desert the bloodstained king. Phegeus of Athens, bringing these words, stood before him, indeed peaceable with boughs of innocent olive, yet he stirs up war and threatens war, rumbling loudly and far too mindful of the one who sent him, and repeating that he is now almost, now with his cohorts to cover the fields in the midst, he stood, the Theban, in an uncertain swell of anxieties, and the threats waver, and his former anger grows lukewarm.

reuse.text: at quibus arvorum studiumque insontis aratri, hos stimulant magnaque ratem per lustra viasque visi laude canunt manifesto in lumine Fauni silvarumque deae atque elatis cornibus Amnes.
reuse.text_original: at quibus arvorum studiumque insontis aratri, / hos stimulant magnaque ratem per lustra viasque / visi laude canunt manifesto in lumine Fauni / silvarumque deae atque elatis cornibus Amnes.
reuse.text_english: But those in whom there is a passion for the fields and for the guiltless plough, these are spurred on; and, as they are seen, they sing of the raft through the years and roads with great praise, in clear light, along with Fauni, the goddesses of the woods, and the Rivers with uplifted horns.
